column1: TS: how do you narrow a union of object types?
column2:
The `in` operator is a type guard — test a key unique to one branch:
  if ("nameSender" in sender) { sender.nameSender }   // narrowed to branch A
  else                        { sender.companySender } // narrowed to branch B
  sender.phoneSender  // shared by BOTH branches -> no narrowing needed
vs `if (obj.nameSender && ...)` on a bag-of-optionals: same runtime test, but the
compiler learns nothing. `in` checks AND narrows.

column1: Zod: 'either A or B' — union, flat+refine, or discriminatedUnion?
column2:
Match the KEY structure the producer actually sends:
  ONE key, two shapes      -> z.union([A, B]) on the VALUE. XOR is inherent, no refine.
                              .optional() works (the value can be undefined).
  SIBLING keys, one of two -> flat z.object + .refine(!!a !== !!b). Optionality on the KEYS
                              (.optional() on a union would apply to the whole object).
  literal tag on the wire  -> z.discriminatedUnion("type", [...]). Best errors.
Union tradeoff: must match a branch EXACTLY or you get a vague "invalid union" 400.

column1: Whose payload shape do you model in a schema?
column2:
The REAL producer's — verify by reading the actual client, not the tidiest/nearest one.
Real case: the bot's /api/notify client is an old PHP site's jQuery, NOT the React app
(which posts to a different backend). Modelling on React produced a schema that would
400 every live request. Identify the producer BEFORE writing the schema.

column1: What's the prior when existing code contradicts your model?
column2:
"They know something I don't" — working code is EVIDENCE, especially when two places
independently agree.
Real case: two endpoints used whatsappSender vs whatsAppSender. Looked like a typo;
it was two different producers. "Fixing" it would silently drop the field — and a
.default(false) makes the absence look intentional. Silent, not loud.
